hook.line: Vale's family is asking who everyone in the photos is. Tomás points at Hernando and says *un amigo de mí*. Polite smiles. Spanish has a word for of mine, and it isn't *de mí*.
hook.es: Hernando es un amigo mío de Bogotá.
hook.en: Hernando is a friend of mine from Bogotá.

examples.es: Tu celular es negro. El mío es azul.
examples.en: Your phone is black. Mine is blue. (to a friend)

examples.es: Mis papás viven en Toronto. ¿Y los tuyos?
examples.en: My parents live in Toronto. And yours? (to a friend)

examples.es: Una prima mía trabaja en Medellín.
examples.en: A cousin of mine works in Medellín.

rule:
Same owner, two shapes, two places.

*mi*, *tu*, *su* (and *mis*, *tus*, *sus*): right in front of the thing, never alone. *mi amigo*, *mis papás*.

*mío*, *tuyo*, *suyo*: everywhere else. After the thing: *un amigo mío*. After *es*: *es mío*. With *el* or *la* when the thing is dropped: *el mío*.

So the test is simple: is the thing right after? Then *mi*. No thing after? Then *mío*.

The meaning shift is the same as in English. *Es mi amigo* is my friend, the one we both know about. *Es un amigo mío* is a friend of mine, one of several.

Two things Spanish never says: *es mi* with nothing after, and *el mi libro*. The short one never takes *el*; the long one needs it when it stands in for a thing.
smallPrint: Teachers call *mi*, *tu*, *su* unstressed possessives and *mío*, *tuyo*, *suyo* stressed possessives.

options: That's my suitcase. Yours is the red one.
That's your suitcase. Mine is the red one.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *mi* or *mío* and type the whole sentence: Es un amigo ___.
yourTurn.why: Nothing comes after, so the long form: *mío*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *mi* or *mío* and type the whole sentence: Hernando es ___ amigo.
yourTurn.why: The thing comes right after, so the short form: *mi*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *mi* or *mía* and type the whole sentence: ¿La llave? Es ___.
yourTurn.why: No thing after *es*, so the long form, matching *llave*: *mía*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: A cousin of mine works in Medellín. (a woman cousin)
yourTurn.answer: Una prima mía trabaja en Medellín.
yourTurn.why: Of mine is *mía* after the noun, matching *prima*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say to a friend: My parents live in Toronto. And yours?
yourTurn.answer: Mis papás viven en Toronto. ¿Y los tuyos?
yourTurn.why: *Mis* goes in front of *papás*; yours alone is *los tuyos*.

yourTurn.prompt: Drop the phone and just say mine: *Mi celular es azul.*
yourTurn.why: With no thing after, *mi* becomes *el mío*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make Hernando a friend of yours, one of several: *Hernando es mi amigo.*
yourTurn.why: A friend of mine is *un amigo mío*.

pitfalls.why: Almost. *Mi* needs a thing after it; alone, it's *mío*.
Spanish never says of me for owning; *mío* after the noun does the job.
The short form never takes *el*: just *mi libro*.

pitfalls.wrong: Tu celular es negro. Mi es azul.
pitfalls.right: Tu celular es negro. El mío es azul.
pitfalls.why: Standing in for the phone, mine is *el mío*.

personal: Name someone close to you with *mi*, then someone you know less well with *mío* or *mía*: *Mi hermana vive en… Un amigo mío trabaja en…*
